summary:
Chocó stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, same-sex marriage has been available since April 2016 and joint adoption since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

No Chocó-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding departs from that national position, so the department is assessed at the national score. What distinguishes the department is who holds the power to enforce order. Chocó sits in the country's frontier belt, where 'orden público' regimes mean armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct, and Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report documents the territorial expansion of violence alongside an insufficient state response, with trans women displaced from departments such as Chocó because of their gender identity by the same armed actors that displace others.

The gap between the national framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one count put 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone. The Guardian reported eight trans women killed between February and April 2024 and 41 killed over 2023. CNN's follow-up in the 'As Equals' series, published on 6 August 2025, reported that the killings continued at the hands of armed gangs after the assault on Sara Millerey shocked the country, and framed being queer in parts of the country as signing your own death sentence.

Where armed groups hold territory the threat is announced before it is carried out. In Caquetá department, armed groups ran a "social cleansing" campaign whose flyers, circulated on the streets and through WhatsApp, named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets and threatened a further wave. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. In Guajira department, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond sex work, and discrimination limits trans women there mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Targeted killings also occur in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Protection machinery exists and has been used. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern. A Colombian court has also ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern that governs Chocó is national rather than local, and the two departments where armed groups have advertised their targets in advance, Caquetá and Guajira, are cited as illustrations of the same frontier dynamic that reaches Chocó. Neither is treated as evidence about Chocó itself.

The distance between Colombia's statutory position and its enforcement is the central turbulence factor. Notarised marker change, constitutional self-recognition and marriage equality coexist with a homicide count that armed groups announce by flyer, and the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 assessment made exactly that disconnection its finding rather than treating the reforms as a description of conditions on the ground.

Violence against trans people in Colombia is not confined to territories under armed-group control. The Millerey killing in Bello, Antioquia, and the CNN reporting of August 2025 show the same outcome in an ordinary urban setting, so a visitor cannot treat the absence of armed-group presence as a reduction in risk to baseline.

Colombia's treatment of conflict-driven anti-LGBT violence as gender persecution before the Special Jurisdiction for Peace is unusual in the region and gives victims a route that ordinary homicide prosecution does not. Whether that machinery reaches a visitor is a different question from whether it exists.
localsOnly:
Colombian residents change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015 and free of the bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments that judges previously ordered. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-recognition without surgery.

A 2011 statute bans discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, and a national LGBTI policy text covers rights in public education, health care, prisons and status as victims of armed conflict, stating that national entities may not refuse to recognise same-sex couples. Victim-of-armed-conflict status is the element of that framework with direct bearing on residents of Chocó, where trans women have been displaced by armed actors.

National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained before the legislature in 2025, so residents are governed by the existing notarial route and constitutional case law rather than by a single consolidated statute.

Trans detainees have judicial protection: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and set standards for the prison system. Residents held in custody in Chocó fall under that ruling and under the prison element of the national LGBTI policy.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Chocó-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding is sourced. The English-language department article yields nothing usable, and no Chocó homicide figure, armed-group incident or displacement case appears in the material assembled here; the department's assessment therefore rests on the national record plus the frontier-enforcement context.

The Caribe Afirmativo 2025 report on territorial expansion of violence and insufficient state response is carried from the department's prior context but is not itself present in the current source inventory, so its specific figures for Chocó remain unverified here.

Whether 'orden público' arrangements formally apply across Chocó's municipalities, and which armed groups currently operate there, are not established by the sources in hand. The Caquetá and Guajira flyer campaigns are documented for those departments and are not evidence of activity inside Chocó.

The status of the comprehensive trans law pending before Colombia's legislature in 2025 is unresolved in this material: no source records whether it was enacted, amended or stalled.
